topic: A week of tech outages and a nationwide FAA ground stop: inherited 'very old equipment,' or a botched upgrade and a presidential shrug?
question: Was the Nov. 13 ground stop, and the week of outages around it, the product of decades-old systems the administration inherited, or of its own upgrade work, staffing cuts and a dismissive response?
summary:
On Friday, Nov. 13, the FAA halted departures nationwide for about four hours and 20 minutes, the longest stop since 9/11. Microsoft, Chase, United and an NSA classified network also went down within days. President Trump blamed 'very, very old equipment that had a heart attack' and said Pete Buttigieg 'ruined the system.' He told Americans to relax and said he takes no responsibility. Democrats say the administration's own upgrade triggered the failure, and that it gutted the federal cyber agency, CISA. At Wednesday's House hearing, intelligence chief Jay Clayton testified that the outages were separate technical failures, not an attack.

The evidence splits. The trigger was a new router installed during a copper-to-fiber upgrade, which flooded the network within eight minutes and overwhelmed older parts. That makes both 'old equipment' and 'their upgrade' half right. The FAA's systems were badly aged long before 2025, as a 2024 GAO audit shows, so 'Buttigieg ruined it' does not hold. CISA really did lose about a third of its staff, but nothing ties these outages to that, and Rep. Dan Goldman's claim that it was cut to hide election fraud has no support. Both parties' intelligence leaders, including Democrat Mark Warner, see no cyberattack.

What the evidence cannot yet settle is the root cause: investigators have not said whether the installation, the router or the network design failed.
verdict: Leans slightly left, close to even. Each side has one solid fact and one overreach. The right is correct that the FAA's systems were aging long before this administration, and that no evidence shows a coordinated attack. But 'Buttigieg ruined the system' is unsupported, and 'old equipment' omits that a new router set off the failure. The left is correct that CISA lost about a third of its staff and that the failure came during the administration's upgrade. But it has no evidence tying CISA cuts to these outages. The root cause is still unknown.
verificationNote: The appropriation was read in Public Law 119-21 on GovInfo, and the 2024 GAO audit on gao.gov. Hearing quotes come from The Hill (read via Yahoo), Fox News and ABC News; the C-SPAN clip was not viewed. Reuters, The Guardian, the FAA newsroom, Congress.gov, the Senate Commerce site, the Washington Times and the Honolulu Star-Advertiser could not be fetched (403 or blocked), and CNN returned 451, so CNN reporting was read through syndicated copies. A Daily Wire report quotes Transportation Secretary Duffy saying 'the router' dated to 2001, which conflicts with every other account of a newly installed router; it is flagged, not resolved. Trump's 'relax' remark is sourced to Fox News's live coverage, and his 'It's life' remark to a single outlet.

left.label: Their upgrade, their shrug
left.framing: The administration was running the upgrade that took down the nation's air traffic system, had already pushed out more than 1,000 federal cyber defenders, and then told Americans to 'relax' while the president said he takes no responsibility. Before Congress hands over $50 billion, Democrats want an accounting.
left.strongestPoint: The ground stop began within eight minutes of a new router going in during the administration's own copper-to-fiber work, and CISA's workforce fell from about 3,400 to 2,200 under Trump. Asking how $12.5 billion was spent before approving $50 billion is a point Senate Republican leader John Thune also presses.
left.weakestPoint: No evidence links CISA's cuts to any of these outages, and Rep. Goldman's claim that CISA was cut to hide election fraud is baseless. Buttigieg's claim to have 'launched' the copper transition is overstated: the work that failed belongs to an L3Harris contract dating to 2002.

right.label: Old systems, no attack
right.framing: The FAA has run on decades-old equipment for years, and the previous administration let it decay. The outages were separate technical failures, not an attack, and flights resumed within hours. The fix is the new air traffic control system, and Congress needs to fund it.
right.strongestPoint: The FAA's own 2023 assessment, audited by GAO in 2024, rated 105 of its 138 air traffic systems unsustainable or potentially so, and both parties' intelligence leaders, Democrat Mark Warner included, see no cyberattack behind the outages.
right.weakestPoint: 'Very old equipment that had a heart attack' leaves out that a newly installed router set off the failure, and 'Buttigieg ruined the system' ignores decay spanning several administrations. Disclaiming all responsibility while blaming the contractor and a predecessor, before the cause is known, is spin.

facts.claim: The Nov. 13 ground stop was caused by 'very, very old equipment that had a heart attack.'
facts.evidence: AP: a Juniper router 'installed during an upgrade in El Dorado, Arkansas' sent thousands of inquiries every few seconds, 'overwhelming older network components'; it caused unstable signals at 17 of 22 key centers. CNBC: the new router began transmitting too much data 'within eight minutes of being installed.'
facts.explanation: Both halves are true: a new device triggered the flood, and older parts failed under it. Calling it an old-equipment 'heart attack' omits the trigger. The router's maker says it worked as configured, and the root cause is undetermined. A Daily Wire report has Duffy dating 'the router' to 2001, which conflicts with all other accounts.

facts.claim: Much of the FAA's air traffic control equipment was badly outdated before this administration took office.
facts.evidence: GAO, Sept. 2024: of the FAA's 138 air traffic control systems, 51 (37 percent) were rated unsustainable and 54 (39 percent) potentially unsustainable. The audit's title: 'FAA Actions Are Urgently Needed to Modernize Aging Systems.'
facts.explanation: The ratings come from the FAA's own 2023 assessment, made under Biden, and describe decay that built up over decades. That supports the right's point that the administration inherited a fragile system. It does not show what caused this particular failure.

facts.evidence: Trump, Nov. 16: 'Buttigieg ruined the system. He totally ruined it.' FactCheck.org: Trump's plan largely extends NextGen, begun in 2003; the 2021 infrastructure law gave air traffic control $5 billion, about $3 billion spent by 2024. A White House spokesperson said the Biden DOT 'did nothing.'
facts.explanation: The aging GAO describes accumulated across several administrations of both parties, and the NextGen effort predates Buttigieg by almost two decades. Biden's DOT did spend money and awarded a new network contract. Fair criticism is that his tenure did not fix the problem; 'ruined' has no supporting evidence.

facts.claim: Buttigieg launched the FAA's move off copper wire, and the Trump administration's execution of it triggered the breakdown.
facts.evidence: Buttigieg: 'I launched a project to transition the FAA's communications system from copper wire to a modern network.' Washington Technology, March 2023: Verizon won the $2.4 billion FENS contract, replacing the FTI contract L3Harris has held since 2002. Fox: the failure came while L3Harris was replacing aging copper lines with fiber.
facts.explanation: His department did award the replacement network contract in 2023. But the copper-to-fiber work that failed runs under L3Harris's older contract, now 70 percent complete per the company. The failure did occur during work this administration oversees, though whether installation or equipment was at fault is unsettled.

facts.claim: The week's outages were separate technical failures, not a coordinated or state-sponsored cyberattack.
facts.evidence: Clayton, Nov. 18: 'These are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.' Sen. Mark Warner (D) told the Financial Times there is 'no indication' of a cyberattack. Stated causes: a Microsoft update bug, a Chase software bug, NSA patching, and the FAA router.
facts.explanation: Each company or agency gave a distinct technical cause, and leaders of both parties agree. Some Republicans dissent: Rep. Nick LaLota said the events seem 'beyond coincidences,' and Marjorie Taylor Greene tied them to the midterms, without evidence. Confidence is medium because classified assessments cannot be checked and investigations continue.

facts.claim: The federal cyber agency, CISA, has lost about a third of its workforce under Trump.
facts.evidence: Rep. Walkinshaw at the hearing: CISA had 3,400 employees at the start of the administration; Mullin testified in June it was down to 2,200 but needed 2,800. Nextgov: 'roughly 3,300' to 'about 2,200.' DHS, defending the cuts, said the Biden-era CISA had 'a ballooning budget.'
facts.explanation: The decline is not disputed; DHS defends it rather than denying it. Mullin, who arrived in March, said he 'wasn't there' for the cuts and that CISA is now hiring. Starting figures differ slightly, 3,300 or 3,400.

facts.claim: CISA's staff cuts helped cause the outages, and were made because the president 'didn't want election fraud to be uncovered.'
facts.evidence: Rep. Goldman: 'CISA is way down because the president didn't want election fraud to be uncovered.' CBS: the NSA outage followed urgent PHP patching; the FAA stop was a hardware problem, not a software flaw. Microsoft and Chase cited their own update and software bugs.
facts.explanation: None of the identified causes involves a system CISA runs; the FAA network is run by the FAA and its contractors. Reduced cyber capacity is a real general concern, which former CISA head Jen Easterly raises. But no evidence ties the cuts to these failures, and the election-fraud motive is unsupported.

facts.claim: The $12.5 billion Congress provided in 2025 does not fund a replacement of the FAA's telecommunications network.
facts.evidence: Public Law 119-21, Sec. 40003: '$4,750,000,000 for telecommunications infrastructure modernization and systems upgrades,' available until Sept. 30, 2029. Fox reports Duffy saying the $12.5 billion does not fund a replacement telecom network. AP: the FAA's request has nearly doubled, to $50 billion.
facts.explanation: The law sets aside $4.75 billion specifically for telecom modernization, so 'no telecom money' is wrong; whether it suffices for a full replacement is a judgment. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican, wants details on how earlier funds were spent, and Newsweek reports the extra $20 billion has not been itemized.

powerLens.thesis: Accountability for air traffic failures tends to land on the other party's transportation secretary. In January 2023 a contractor error caused the first nationwide ground stop since 9/11; House Republicans later called it a 'preventable malfunction' in a resolution seeking Buttigieg's resignation. Today the same kind of event happens on a Republican's watch, and the roles reverse.

precedent.case: The NOTAM outage and nationwide ground stop, Jan. 11, 2023
precedent.what: The FAA said contractors working to 'correct synchronization between the live primary database and a backup database' unintentionally deleted files. Departures halted nationwide; airlines canceled more than 1,300 flights and delayed nearly 10,000.
precedent.mirror: Then, a contractor error on an old system under a Democratic secretary drew Republican calls for accountability at the top. Now, a contractor-involved failure under a Republican secretary draws Democratic demands, while the president says he takes no responsibility.

flips.then: March 2023: a resolution led by Rep. Mike Waltz sought Buttigieg's resignation, citing the ground stop caused by 'a preventable malfunction.'
flips.now: Nov. 16, 2026: Trump says 'I don't take any responsibility' for the ground stop, noting Duffy was in charge, and blames 'very, very old equipment.'

flips.then: February 2023, after his own ground stop: the need was to 'pick up the pace on FAA's wholesale system modernization,' with Congress moving funding faster.
flips.now: November 2026: the administration has 'failed to explain why their execution of it triggered the worst FAA communications breakdown this century,' and owes an accounting before more money.

powerLens.longRun: Strip out the party labels and the record is one of slow decay and slow repair across every administration since NextGen began in 2003. Each failure gets pinned on whoever holds DOT that day. Expect the next ground stop to be blamed the same way; the measure that matters is whether funded upgrades get installed safely and audited.
powerLens.appliedToScore: Republicans lose reasoning credit for disclaiming responsibility for a failure of the kind they pinned on Buttigieg in 2023. Buttigieg loses some for treating 'old system, needs money' as an excuse now that it is the other side's. The needle rests on present facts: a new router trigger, an aged network, real CISA cuts, and no attack.

pattern.thesis: The ground stop is not a one-off. It follows a string of air traffic communications failures across two administrations, and it arrived in a week when patching for AI-found software flaws also knocked systems offline. Judging it alone invites blaming one person; judging it in sequence points at fragile, patched-together infrastructure.

campaigns.what: Contractors unintentionally deleted files, causing the first nationwide ground stop since 9/11.
105 of the FAA's 138 air traffic control systems rated unsustainable or potentially unsustainable.
Controllers lost radar and radio contact with Newark traffic for up to about 90 seconds; the FAA cited a 'telecommunications outage.'
An internal network went down after urgent patching of PHP flaws that AI helped uncover; Clayton said the patching caused some systems 'to not come back up.'

pattern.takeaway: The recurring question: can old networks absorb rapid upgrades and patching without breaking, and who is accountable when they don't? The 'one-off' tell is any account that names a single villain, whether Buttigieg, Duffy, a contractor or a foreign hacker, without mentioning the decades of deferred repair underneath.

notAdjudicable: How much a president or cabinet secretary should personally own an operational failure by an agency or contractor is a judgment about leadership, not a factual question.
Whether $50 billion for air traffic control is worth its cost compared with other spending is a fiscal priority question.
Whether a smaller CISA with more automation is an acceptable trade-off against a larger federal cyber workforce is a question about the size and role of government.
Whether a cabinet secretary should attend a football game the day after a national disruption is a question of optics and propriety, not fact.
biasWatch: The bias here is agency detection: a cluster of failures feels designed, so people reach for a culprit that fits their side. On the right, that means Buttigieg, or saboteurs tied to the midterms; on the left, Trump's cuts or a cover-up. The evidence so far points to separate technical failures on aging, heavily patched systems. The tell: watch whether someone's explanation of the outages would change if the other party ran DOT. If 'old equipment' was an excuse in 2023 and a diagnosis in 2026, or the reverse, the label is doing the work.
